title: AI labs are buying data from dead startups to train their models
gist: A new market has emerged in which dying startups sell code and workspace data (Slack, Notion, email) to AI labs as training material, brokered by firms like SimpleClosure and Sunset. Prices are set by speculative 'research theses' with no published evidence yet on real-data gains, and legal and privacy exposure is significant.

insights.claim: Startup shutdowns are rising 26% to 56% annually per Carta and AngelList estimates, which has spawned an end-of-life services ecosystem including coaches, 'death doulas' and legal/tax wind-down firms.
insights.speaker: Matthew King
insights.so_what: A growing supply of failed startups is a structural source of cheap training data and a marker of venture-cycle stress.
insights.quote: Estimates from Carta and AngelList show shutdowns rising between 26% and 56% annually

insights.claim: SimpleClosure added data sales in April; its Asset Hub has handled over 150 deals, expects to return over $10 million to startups by end of 2026, and 47% of its deals now include code or data sales.
insights.speaker: Matthew King
insights.so_what: Shows a fast-normalising, though still small, revenue line: about $10M across 150+ deals is roughly tens of thousands per deal.
insights.quote: Asset Hub has handled over 150 deals and expects to return over $10 million to startups by the end of 2026.

insights.claim: A crypto startup founder netted about $25,000 for his code base and likely about $15,000 more for Google, Notion, Figma and Slack workspace data after a 2.5-year run, illustrating the typical small-ticket scale of a startup data sale.
insights.speaker: Matthew King
insights.so_what: Typical startup-scale payouts are small; value concentrates in large corporate archives.
insights.quote: At least all that stuff we were doing for two and a half years is worth something to someone somewhere

insights.claim: Sunset values a dying company's assets by head count, years in operation, data volume and how the team used its tools, and likens 'operational exhaust' data to wood shavings turned into particle board.
insights.speaker: Matthew King
insights.so_what: Byproduct data is being reclassified as an asset class with its own valuation heuristics, which could extend to live companies.
insights.quote: This operational exhaust data is like the wood shavings that everyone thought had no value, but it actually has a ton.

insights.claim: Buyers include foundation AI labs, vendors that build simulated workspaces for AI training, and mature tech companies training their own models.
insights.speaker: Matthew King
insights.so_what: Demand is broad across the AI stack, not just the largest labs.

themes.theme: Why real workplace data is wanted

insights.claim: Demand for defunct-company data emerged last year because AI labs hit the limits of public and synthetic datasets.
insights.speaker: Matthew King
insights.so_what: Data scarcity is pushing labs to pay for proprietary enterprise exhaust, a possible tailwind for data-rich distressed assets.
insights.quote: AI training labs hit the limits of public and synthetic datasets

insights.claim: Surge AI uses archives to build reinforcement-learning gyms where clients' agents practice tasks such as debugging complex IT architecture or drafting appellate briefs, and prizes archives with disagreements and tricky judgment calls.
insights.speaker: Matthew King
insights.so_what: The workflow-agent training race favors messy realistic human interaction data over clean data.

insights.claim: One company's Slack history, if it captures varied and deep conversations, can be worth more than another's Slack, email and calendars combined, so value depends on data richness rather than volume.
insights.speaker: Nick Heiner (cited by Matthew King)
insights.so_what: Pricing power sits with archives rich in judgment and conflict, not with sheer size.
insights.locator: Heiner explains that one company's Slack history

insights.claim: Real archives avoid common synthetic-world errors such as references to dates that don't exist, but no company has released tests comparing real-world-data training against alternatives, so the performance gain is unproven.
insights.speaker: Matthew King
insights.so_what: Buyers are paying on faith; published ablations would be a catalyst that reprices the market.
insights.quote: No company has yet released tests comparing results of real-world data training with the alternatives.

insights.claim: Buyers quote wildly different prices because valuations rest on subjective 'research theses' about how many useful tasks come from a given amount of data, such as 100,000 lines of code.
insights.speaker: Matthew King
insights.so_what: Price dispersion implies founders may be underpaid and that arbitrage exists for informed intermediaries.

insights.claim: In August, in Spirit Airlines' bankruptcy, Google outbid AI data company Mercor for decades of carrier data, including 100 million emails, 500 million Teams messages and 176,000 employee records, for $10 million.
insights.speaker: Matthew King
insights.so_what: Big tech is a bidder in bankruptcy courts; bankruptcy filings now carry a data-asset angle for creditors' recoveries.
insights.quote: Google outbid the AI data company Mercor to buy the carrier’s decades of data

insights.claim: Bloomberg reported in September that SpaceX's AI unit is weighing purchasing data from struggling startups, suggesting more well-capitalised bidders are entering.
insights.speaker: Matthew King
insights.so_what: More buyers should support prices, supporting the shutdown-services niche.

insights.claim: Such data is described as 'legally radioactive' because emails and calendars hold private details like doctor appointments and school pickups; Spirit's flight attendants' union objected on privacy grounds, and the market is a 'Wild West' only starting to move to licensing and vetted use.
insights.speaker: Matthew King
insights.so_what: Litigation or regulatory action could create liability for buyers and taint models trained on such data.

insights.claim: Proceeds from wind-down data sales typically go to senior creditors and investors rather than employees, and an Emory law professor calls it 'captured capital' while noting there's no federal law banning sales of workers' data without consent.
insights.speaker: Matthew King
insights.so_what: Potential regulatory and labor-policy flashpoint; a federal consent rule would shrink supply.
insights.quote: there’s no federal law banning such sales

insights.claim: Founders have little visibility into who buys their data or what for, and little assurance of a fair price, limiting the appeal of the market.
insights.speaker: Matthew King
insights.so_what: Information asymmetry favors brokers and buyers over sellers.
insights.locator: While many see this new market

insights.claim: The author expects data prices to stabilize in the coming year unless an AI bubble pops first, with the 'undertakers' appraising what remains either way.
insights.speaker: Matthew King
insights.so_what: Data pricing is a second-order exposure to AI-capex sentiment.
insights.quote: unless an AI bubble pops first
